text: Three weeks into November, the budget alert from Lesson 30 fires: Briarcliff's resource group has already crossed 80% of its $150 monthly budget, on day 19. That's not a surprise bill at month-end — it's a warning with time left to act. The alert says how much is being spent. It doesn't say why, and finding why is this lesson.

The budget itself just confirms what the alert already said. To find the cause, you need spend broken down by resource, not a resource-group total. A Cost Management query grouped by ResourceId ranks every resource by actual spend this month, and one line sits far above the rest: a VM called loadtest-vm1 that nobody on the ticket even remembers creating.

az vm show reports Standard_D4s_v3, running — a 4-vCPU size, far bigger than anything else in this environment, and it's been running continuously since a load test two weeks ago that nobody deallocated afterward. Its disk turns out to be Premium_LRS, priced for latency-sensitive production work, attached to what was only ever meant to be a one-off test box.

The load test is over, so the fix stops the bleeding and brings the resource back in line with what it's actually for. Deallocate stops compute billing immediately. Resizing down to Standard_B2s and re-tiering the disk to StandardSSD_LRS means the next time this VM is needed, it starts up costing a fraction of what it quietly cost for two unattended weeks.

The sequence that found it: a budget alert on day 19, a cost-by-resource query that singled out loadtest-vm1, az vm show confirming an oversized VM running unattended, az disk list confirming an oversized disk tier to match, and a three-command fix. Narrowing down beats guessing, every time.

That's the whole incident, start to finish, using nothing but the governance, compute, and monitoring habits from earlier in this course. The last lesson in this chapter — and in this course — ties all seven chapters together in one review.
